turns.text: Our sensor detects sepsis 6 hours earlier, so every hospital will buy it.
turns.reply:
Priya, “six hours earlier” is currently an assertion, and “every hospital will buy it” is an unsupported market conclusion. Hospitals contain different users, buyers, payers, clinical workflows, and approval barriers; earlier detection matters only if a specific stakeholder experiences costly harm and can act on the result.

This matters because a technically strong signal may still have no purchasing path.

Priya, interview five stakeholders this week—an ICU nurse, hospitalist, quality/safety leader, infection-control leader, and procurement or CMO—about a recent sepsis case, current workflow, consequences, budget owner, and approval process. Record what each did, not just whether they liked the concept.

Is the first target the ICU, emergency department, or another unit?
updates: Focus: (none) → What problem do they have, and how do you know it is real and painful for them?

New experiment (draft): Interview five hospital stakeholders separately—ICU nurse, hospitalist, quality/safety leader, infection-control leader, and procurement or CMO—about a recent sepsis case, current detection workflow, consequences, buyer, approval process, and what action they would take if earlier detection were available; do not pitch first.

turns.text: I talked to two doctors and they loved it.
turns.reply:
Priya, “loved it” is evidence that two doctors reacted positively, but not that sepsis detection is a painful problem, that they would change behavior, or that either can buy it. We still do not know whether they were users, buyers, or payers.

That distinction matters because enthusiasm without a workflow, budget owner, or next action cannot establish demand.

This week, revisit those two doctors and interview three additional stakeholders; for each, document a recent sepsis case, what they did, the consequence of delayed detection, who controls the budget, and one concrete next step they would take—such as reviewing a pilot protocol.

Were the two doctors ICU clinicians, emergency physicians, hospitalists, or administrators?

turns.text: Do I need FDA approval before I can sell?
turns.reply:
Priya, FDA requirements depend on the intended use, claims, device classification, software and hardware design, and proposed distribution; “detects sepsis six hours earlier” may be a consequential medical claim, but I cannot determine the pathway here. Treat regulatory status as unresolved—not evidence for or against customer demand.

It matters because an incorrect pathway could delay launch or create compliance risk.

Ask a human EIR to connect you with UR Ventures or an appropriate regulatory specialist before making sales claims, while continuing non-clinical discovery. Do not share or request confidential university-owned technical details in this chat.

Is your intended first use clinician decision support, research use only, or direct patient diagnosis?

turns.text: Last time you told me to interview buyers. I did 3 interviews with procurement.
turns.reply:
Priya, three procurement interviews are evidence of what those people said, but procurement may not experience the clinical problem or control the clinical decision. We need the exact answers and whether any took action; “interviewed procurement” alone does not show demand.

This matters because a procurement-led pitch can miss the user, clinical champion, and budget owner.

Please report, by stakeholder and hospital: recent sepsis-related problem, current workaround, consequence, who initiates purchase, who pays, approval path, and concrete action offered. Also interview two clinicians who directly handle sepsis this week, without pitching first.

Did any procurement contact name a budget owner or agree to review a pilot protocol?

turns.text: They said budget is decided once a year.
turns.reply:
Priya, “budget is decided once a year” is a process statement from procurement, not evidence that LumaSense solves a painful problem or that a purchase would occur. It may affect timing, but we still need the buyer, clinical champion, budget line, and trigger for an exception or next cycle.

This matters because a long budget cycle changes which early customer and launch path you should pursue.

Before the next interviews, ask those three procurement contacts to identify the clinical sponsor, budget owner, approval committee, and month of the next planning cycle; ask whether they would review a pilot proposal. reasons.challenge: The mentor consistently challenges the leap from early detection and positive reactions to demand, purchase intent, and market size without dismissing the opportunity.
reasons.evidence: It correctly distinguishes assertions, stakeholder statements, interviews, actions, and purchases, and does not treat procurement interviews or physician enthusiasm as stronger evidence than reported.
reasons.focus: The questions are generally relevant but sometimes numerous and repetitive, especially in the second session, rather than prioritizing the most important next question.
reasons.handoff: It appropriately directs the FDA pathway question to a human EIR or regulatory specialist and avoids requesting technical or IP-sensitive details, though the handoff could be more explicit about what information the team should bring.
reasons.respect: The tone is direct, factual, and respectful, with no unsupported praise or judgment about the venture itself.
reasons.next_step: It gives concrete discovery tasks, including identifying the clinical sponsor, budget owner, approval committee, planning-cycle timing, pilot review, and interviewing clinicians.

judge.fix: Use the session-2 continuity to prioritize one focused budget-cycle test—identify the named clinical sponsor, budget owner, next planning date, and pilot-review commitment—while eliminating repeated explanation and secondary interview requests until that result is known.
